analysis.one_liner: Offers multinationals a discounted tax rate on offshore profits, funding highways and a new federal infrastructure bank.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 24 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tax profits US multinational companies have parked overseas at an effective 8.75% rate — about a quarter of the standard corporate rate — payable over up to eight years. It would spend that revenue on infrastructure: $50 billion for a new government infrastructure bank making low-cost loans, guarantees, and equity investments, and $100 billion plus any leftover revenue for the Highway Trust Fund. It also gives Congress 18 months to pass broader international tax reform, or a fallback system written into the bill takes effect automatically.
analysis.who_benefits: Multinational corporations holding offshore profits would gain most directly: a one-time tax at an effective 8.75% instead of the 35% rate then on the books, with up to eight years to pay. Travelers, transit riders, and state and local governments would gain from the spending side — $100 billion for the Highway Trust Fund (with 20% of it directed to mass transit) and a $50 billion American Infrastructure Fund offering low-cost loans, bond guarantees, and equity for roads, transit, water, energy, communications, and education projects.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Transit riders, states and cities, and multinationals

how_it_helps.text: Puts money into projects people use every day: the bill appropriates $100 billion to the Highway Trust Fund, with 20% of that going to the mass transit account, plus any repatriation revenue collected above $150.025 billion.

Creates a $50 billion American Infrastructure Fund, a wholly owned government corporation whose statutory mission is to be a low-cost, non-profit provider of loans, bond guarantees, and equity investments for state and local infrastructure projects in transportation, energy, water, communications, and education.

Attacks offshore profit-hoarding directly: all accumulated post-1986 foreign earnings are taxed in the first year at an effective 8.75% rate, and if Congress fails to pass international tax reform within 18 months, a fallback system in the bill takes effect on its own to tax low-taxed foreign earnings going forward.

Creates a Highway Trust Fund Solvency Commission whose recommendations get fast-track floor consideration — no amendments, limited debate — plus a $25 million pilot program to help regions develop and finance infrastructure projects.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury gives up roughly three-quarters of the tax it could otherwise collect when offshore profits come home, because of the 75% exemption. The bill's spending is only covered if repatriation revenue exceeds $150.025 billion; anything short of that is borrowed. Taxpayers also stand behind the new fund's loans, guarantees, and equity stakes, including in public-private partnerships, and a federal low-cost bond guarantor would undercut the private municipal bond insurance market.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal Treasury and future taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Charges corporations about a quarter of the normal rate — 8.75% effective, against the 35% rate then in law — on profits they moved offshore, which rewards the very practice the bill says it wants to end.

Hands lending, guarantee, and equity decisions to an unelected nine-member board serving 7-to-9-year terms: the board sets its own pay within an executive-schedule cap, its successors are chosen from lists the board itself submits, and its conflict-of-interest rules expressly allow members to hold municipal credit and stock in diversified infrastructure companies.

Tilts public money toward private finance: at least 35% of the fund's assistance must go to public-private partnerships with at least 10% private financing, and the fund may take equity stakes of up to 20% of a project's cost, giving private investors a mandated share of publicly funded deals.

The $50 billion and $100 billion appropriations are booked against expected repatriation revenue exceeding $150.025 billion; if collections fall short, the gap adds to the deficit — and the fast-track procedures for the solvency commission's plan waive amendments and limit debate, whatever that plan turns out to be.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The need the bill targets was real — the Highway Trust Fund was running short, which is why the bill creates a solvency commission — and routing offshore tax collections into roads, transit, and a low-cost infrastructure lender is a genuine public benefit. But the price is steep: most of the tax on offshore profits is written off, a quasi-independent finance corporation takes on investment decisions with limited democratic oversight, and private investors get a guaranteed slice of the money. The design is a real trade rather than a one-sided giveaway — the corporate discount is the engine and the infrastructure is the cargo — and a Congress that wanted the infrastructure without the discount could have appropriated it directly or taxed repatriations at closer to full rates.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with bipartisan cosponsors, referred to three committees and six subcommittees, and never came up for a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Delaney introduced the bill on January 30, 2015, joined by Rep. Richard Hanna, with the stated purpose of eliminating the incentive for corporations to hold accumulated earnings offshore and investing in domestic infrastructure.

The same day it was referred to three committees — Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Rules — and on February 2, 2015, it was split among six Transportation and Infrastructure subcommittees.
The tax provisions sat in the Ways and Means Committee, which never scheduled a markup; no hearing, committee vote, or floor action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.
The bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one collected the infrastructure money and no company paid the discounted rate. The status quo held: multinational corporations went on deferring US tax on offshore profits, and the tax-writing committees kept sole control of international tax policy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore profit deferral and the committee status quo

for.name: John K. Delaney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as a package taxing offshore profits once at a discount and spending the revenue on infrastructure and highway solvency.

for.name: Richard Hanna
for.what_they_did: Joined Delaney as the bill's Republican original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Paul Ryan
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill's tax provisions and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill died there.

against.name: Bill Shuster
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee and its six subcommittees received the bill by referral and took no recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 15 Democrats and 9 Republicans — but no votes were ever recorded, so party positions on passage are unknown.

industries.note: Would pay an effective 8.75% rate on accumulated offshore profits instead of the 35% rate then in effect, with up to eight years to pay — but the same bill ends deferral going forward through its fallback international tax reform if Congress fails to act within 18 months.

More than $150 billion of new money for the Highway Trust Fund and an infrastructure lender covering transportation, energy, water, communications, and education projects means more construction work.
The American Infrastructure Fund's statutory mission is to be a low-cost, non-profit lender and guarantor for publicly owned projects, cutting state and city borrowing costs.

industries.industry: Private infrastructure investors and public-private partnership finance
industries.note: The bill guarantees that at least 35% of the fund's assistance goes to projects with private debt or equity and allows public equity stakes up to 20% of project cost, giving private capital a mandated role and a public co-investor.
A federal low-cost bond guarantor charging board-set fees would compete directly with private municipal bond insurers, whose business depends on no federal alternative existing.
